Jeremoth
JER-eh-moth
proper noun
Hebrew Yeremoth (H3406), elevations or heights — a plural form from rum (H7311), to be high, to be lifted up, to be exalted.

Biblical Definition

Jeremoth is borne by several men, most of them Levites and most of them keeping something. One is a son of Becher of Benjamin (1Ch 7:8); one a son of Beriah among the heads of the fathers of Benjamin (1Ch 8:14); one is a Merarite Levite of the sons of Mushi — the sons of Mushi; Mahli, and Eder, and Jeremoth, three (1Ch 23:23). Another leads the fifteenth of the twenty-four courses of singers whom David set apart for the service of song in the house of the LORD, each course numbering twelve (1Ch 25:22). Two more appear in Ezra's list of those who had taken strange wives and put them away (Ezr 10:26-27). The name means heights, from rum, to be lifted up. It is the verb of exaltation throughout the Psalms — Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens (Psa 57:5) — and also the verb of the proud heart that Scripture warns against, for the same word describes both the LORD who is high above all nations and the man whose heart is lifted up to his own destruction.

Origin & Era

The name of several men, chiefly Levites, including the leader of the fifteenth course of singers appointed by David. It means heights.

JEREMOTH, Hebrew Yeremoth, elevations, heights; from rum, to be high.

1. A son of Becher, of the tribe of Benjamin.

2. A son of Beriah, among the heads of the fathers of Benjamin at Jerusalem.

3. A Levite of the sons of Mushi, of the house of Merari.

4. The leader of the fifteenth course of the singers in the house of the LORD, he, his sons and his brethren, twelve.

Key Scripture

1Ch 23:23 — "The sons of Mushi; Mahli, and Eder, and Jeremoth, three."

1Ch 8:14 — "And Ahio, Shashak, and Jeremoth,"

Ezr 10:26 — "And of the sons of Elam; Mattaniah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, and Abdi, and Jeremoth, and Eliah."

Ezr 10:27 — "And of the sons of Zattu; Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, and Jeremoth, and Zabad, and Aziza."

Modern Corruption

Music in worship is judged by its effect on the congregation; David ordered it as a ministry of the word, prophesying with harps.

expand to see more

The argument about music in the church is nearly always conducted as a question of taste and effect: what moves people, what draws them, what suits the culture. First Chronicles 25 approaches it from another direction entirely. David and the captains of the host separated the singers to their service, and the text describes what they were doing as prophesying — who prophesied with a harp, to give thanks and to praise the LORD (1Ch 25:3). The singers were ordered into twenty-four courses by lot, trained, numbered, and set under their fathers. It was an office, not an atmosphere.

Two things follow. First, the content governs: sung worship is the word of God returned to God, which is why Paul ties psalms, hymns and spiritual songs directly to the word of Christ dwell[ing] in you richly (Col 3:16). Second, the manner is ordered: trained men, appointed by name, in fixed courses, doing a set work. The principle to recover is that congregational song is a ministry of the word and is to be judged as preaching is judged — by whether what is sung is true, and whether the people are being taught by it — and not by how the room feels afterwards.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Yeremoth (H3406), a plural from rum (H7311), to be high, to be exalted.

expand to see more

Hebrew rum (H7311) — to be high, to rise, to be exalted; Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens (Psa 57:5).

Hebrew Yeremoth (H3406) — borne by Benjamites, Levites and singers; 1 Chronicles 7:8, 8:14, 23:23, 25:22.

Hebrew ramah (H7413) — a height, a high place; the same root, and the name of Samuel's town.

Hebrew naba (H5012) — to prophesy; used of the singers who prophesied with a harp (1Ch 25:3).

Greek psalmos (G5568) — a psalm, a song sung to accompaniment; psalms and hymns and spiritual songs (Col 3:16).

Usage

"“The fifteenth to Jeremoth, he, his sons, and his brethren, were twelve”."
